## Description of the sources

The raw datasets used for this project were downloaded from the official sources (Mendeley Data for the ChatGPT perception survey, and the World Bank for the country income classification). These raw files have been added directly to the GitHub repository of this project. The Github repository can be found at the following link: \[https://github.com/klyfat2/Projet-data-chatgpt.git\]

```{r}
#| message: false
here::i_am("Projet-data-chatgpt.Rproj")
library(here)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(vroom)
library(tidyr)
```

```{r}
#| message: false

survey_data <- vroom(here("data", "survey dataset.csv"), 
                     delim = ";", 
                     locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"))
wb_data <- vroom(here("data", "World Bank Country and Lending Groups .csv"))

```

```{r}
#| message: false

survey_summary <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("File", "Number of rows", "Number of columns", "Numeric variables", "Character variables", "Missing values (NA)"),
  Value = c("survey dataset.csv", 
            nrow(survey_data), 
            ncol(survey_data), 
            survey_data |> select(where(is.numeric)) |> ncol(), 
            survey_data |> select(where(is.character)) |> ncol(), 
            sum(is.na(survey_data)))
)

wb_summary <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("File", "Number of rows", "Number of columns", "Numeric variables", "Character variables", "Missing values (NA)"),
  Value = c("World Bank Country and Lending Groups .csv", 
            nrow(wb_data), 
            ncol(wb_data), 
            wb_data |> select(where(is.numeric)) |> ncol(), 
            wb_data |> select(where(is.character)) |> ncol(), 
            sum(is.na(wb_data)))
)

survey_summary
wb_summary

```

## Description of the main variables

- ChatGPT version : The version of ChatGPT used (subscription or free) may show if the “efficiency” of the AI has an impact
- Economic statut (Q39) : The perceived economic statut is our only way to know the revenu of our sample
- Frequency : Frequency of use may differ depending on gender, academic level, field of study or the version of ChatGPT used 
- Type of uses (Q18) : Such as frequency of use, usages patterns may differ depending on gender, academic level, field of study or the version of ChatGPT used 
- Success in studies (Q35a) : The perceived success in studies is our only indicator of the efficiency of our sample 
- Region : Uses may differ depending on the region
- Income Group : Linked with the economic statut, the income group will allow us to build a scale of real wealth 


## Data Cleaning 

### Gender
```{r}
survey = survey_data |>
  mutate( Q2 = Q2 |> 
            na_if(3) |>
            na_if(4)) |>
  rename(gender = Q2)
```

### Age

```{r}
survey = survey |> 
  mutate(Q3 = if_else(Q3 < 16 | Q3 > 50, NA, Q3)) |> 
  rename(age = Q3)
```

### Rename 

```{r}
survey = survey |> 
  rename(
    nationality = Q1,
    ChatGPT_user = Q13, 
     ChatGPT_version = Q14,
    frequency = Q15,
    ethic_policy = Q20
  )
```

```{r}
wb = wb_data |>
  filter(!is.na(Economy)) |>
  rename(country = Economy) |>
  mutate(country = recode_values(country, 
    "C\xf4te d\x92Ivoire" ~ "Cote d'Ivoire",
    "S\xe3o Tom\xe9 and Pr\xedncipe" ~ "Sao Tome and Príncipe",
    "T\xfcrkiye" ~ "Turkiye",
    default = country 
  ))
```

## Data Joining

### Key variable 

```{r}
survey = survey |>
  rename(country = Q4)
```

```{r}
survey <- survey |> 
  mutate(country = recode_values(country,
    "The Netherlands"          ~ "Netherlands",
    "Turkey"                   ~ "Turkiye",
    "Macedonia"                ~ "North Macedonia",
    "Antigua & Barbuda"        ~ "Antigua and Barbuda",
    "Bosnia & Herzegovina"     ~ "Bosnia and Herzegovina",
    "United States of America" ~ "United States",
    "Cape Verde"               ~ "Cabo Verde",
    "Taiwan"                   ~ "Taiwan, China",
    "The Philippines"          ~ "Philippines",
    "Bahamas"                  ~ "Bahamas, The",
    "Egypt"                    ~ "Egypt, Arab Rep.",
    "Russia"                   ~ "Russian Federation",
    "Gambia"                   ~ "Gambia, The",
    "Czech Republic"           ~ "Czechia",
    "Slovakia"                 ~ "Slovak Republic",
    "Iran"                     ~ "Iran, Islamic Rep.",
    "Palestinian State*"       ~ "West Bank and Gaza",
    "Korea South"              ~ "Korea, Rep.",
    "Korea North"              ~ "Korea, Dem. People's Rep.",
    "Vatican City (Holy See)"  ~ "Vatican", 
    "Other:"                   ~ NA_character_,
    default = country 
  ))
```

### Join 

```{r}
survey = survey|>
  left_join(wb, by = "country")
```

## Description of the research question

The rapid rise of generative AI tools like ChatGPT is changing how university students learn and work. While early studies suggest that AI can act as a "personalized tutor" that helps every student regardless of their background, paid subscriptions create new financial barriers. This thesis sets out to explore a central research question: does generative AI reduce educational inequalities in higher education, or does it reinforce existing economic and gender gaps?

To investigate this question, our upcoming empirical analysis will combine an international student survey with World Bank macroeconomic indicators to test three main hypotheses. 
While basic access to ChatGPT is free, the most powerful models require paid subscriptions. We will test whether access to paid AI depends on both a student's personal wealth and the economic development of their home country.
We will examine whether students from modest backgrounds or competitive fields use paid AI as a strategic investment to improve their grades and job prospects. We will also test whether students who work part-time jobs rely more heavily on AI to save time and manage busy schedules.
We aim to verify whether traditional gender gaps persist in AI adoption, looking at whether men and women differ in their overall usage intensity, their likelihood of paying for Premium versions, and their use of technical tasks like coding and math versus academic writing.
By exploring these three dimensions, this research seeks to understand whether generative AI truly democratizes access to academic support, or if it simply mirrors and amplifies existing social and gender divides in higher education.
